1 Red Flag That AMD Investors Should Be Aware Of Now
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

NVDA

Adanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) investors have enjoyed some incredible gains during 2026. Currently, AMD is the ninth-best-performing component of the S&P 500, returning about 160% so far this year. While that figure was closer to 200% before the most recent sell-off, I think this is a wake-up call for most investors.

The reality is that AMD's stock got way too ahead of itself, and its valuation far outpaces its growth expectations. That is a major red flag for investors, and there are a few items investors need to keep an eye on as to when AMD could be a good buy again (hint: It won't be for a while).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
AMD is gaining ground, but not fast enough

The entire AMD investment thesis circles around AMD catching up to Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and taking market share. On the surface, it appears that AMD is making headway. It has huge projects like OpenAI's computing cluster, which is starting to be delivered, and is powering Meta Muse from Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META). This has all led to stronger growth for AMD, with its data center division reporting $6.7 billion in revenue and growing by 107%. Overall, this helped the company grow its revenue 50% year over year to $11.5 billion in Q2.

Those are strong results that should be celebrated, but the problem is, it just isn't enough to catch Nvidia. During Q2, Nvidia's data center revenue reached $89 billion, up 117% year over year. Overall revenue rose to $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. While AMD appears on the surface to be doing better, the reality is that Nvidia's lead is widening.

What makes matters worse is that Nvidia's Q2 results don't include any revenue from its upcoming generation of Vera Rubin architecture chips. This new generation promises major improvements, and they also cost more than previous generations. This will further exaggerate Nvidia's lead over AMD and eliminate the thesis that AMD is catching up.

But don't tell AMD's stock that, because according to it, AMD has won the AI arms race.

AMD's stock has uncoupled from its business

Over the long term, stocks and business growth are highly correlated. Over the short term, any number of factors can influence a stock's price. This is why long-term investing is easier for individual investors, as we can afford to wait for the business results to influence the stock price as long as we've found a company with a great long-term growth thesis.

Key Stats for Intel Stock

Current Price: $89.85

Target Price (Mid): ~$390

Street Target: ~$118

Potential Total Return: ~336%

Annualized IRR: ~42% / year

What Happened?

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) CEO C.C. Wei signaled on October 15, 2026, that TSMC would support customers who cannot get enough capacity from the EMIB-T packaging of Intel Corporation (INTC). That puts a competitor directly in the path of the foundry business Intel expects to ramp first.

Intel closed at $89.85 on October 16, down 5.79%, in a broad chip selloff that took Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) down 5.95% and Arm Holdings (ARM) down 6.94%. Some outlets also tied Intel's drop to Wei's remarks. On October 14, an explosion at Intel's Kiryat Gat fab in Israel killed two workers, and as of October 16, Intel had not said whether output was affected. Intel reports Q3 results after the close on October 29, per its investor relations materials.

Intel Drawdowns (TIKR)
TSMC Offered Itself as the Backup to Intel's Packaging Push

EMIB-T is Intel's technology for linking AI chips and high-bandwidth memory inside one large package. Wei was answering Morgan Stanley's Charlie Chan, and he called TSMC's CoWoS packaging customers' first choice. TSMC's own lines are tight: in August, Taiwan's Economic Daily News reported some orders spilling from fully booked CoWoS capacity to Intel's Malaysia operations.

EVP and CFO David Zinsner said at an August 26 Deutsche Bank conference that packaging revenue should start ramping in the back half of 2027, ahead of high-volume 14A production in 2028. He expects it to run at around a 40% gross margin and 30% operating margin. Intel has not named a packaging customer, so that timeline rests on management commentary, not disclosed contracts. Intel Foundry lost $10.318 billion at the operating line in fiscal 2025, per TIKR.

Why Packaging Wins Could Delay a 50% Gross Margin

Zinsner still calls a gross margin starting with a 5 the goal, but said Intel is reticent to put a date on it because "some of our businesses actually don't get 50-plus percent gross margins, but they are really high-growth businesses." He put front-end foundry and advanced packaging at around 40% gross margin for now, and many custom ASIC products in the 40s as well.

Intel instead holds each unit to a "Rule of 45," where revenue growth plus operating margin should add up to 45, letting fast growers run thinner margins. Zinsner said not every unit will hit it next year.

Consensus already pencils in the level he won't date. Wall Street models gross margin rising from 36.7% in 2025 to around 54% in 2030, per TIKR, though only seven analysts publish 2030 revenue estimates. Each packaging win adds revenue near a 40% margin, and TSMC competing for the same customers could pressure that pricing. Intel's Q3 guidance midpoint of 42% is up from 39% guided for Q2.

When investors think about AI chipmakers, they may think first of Nvidia or AMD. However, one competitor that most forget about is Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO). Why? It's simple: Broadcom only makes computing units for giant customers, not consumers. However, this is a huge opportunity that shouldn't be ignored, because the growth that Broadcom's management team is guiding for is simply incredible.

If you've got $10,000 sitting around (or any other dollar figure, for that matter), I can think of few better places to invest it, because that $10,000 could be worth $20,000 by the end of 2028.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
What makes Broadcom different?

AMD and Nvidia make graphics processing units (GPUs), parallel processors that are great at handling a wide range of computationally heavy workloads. GPUs don't have a weakness, but their potential often goes underutilized. Countless GPUs have been stuck running a single type of workload throughout their service life, which leaves some of their incredible capabilities wasted. AI hyperscalers would be better off using a purpose-built computing chip in these applications, which is where Broadcom steps in.

Broadcom partners with its hyperscaler clients to design custom AI computing units powered by proprietary chips that only have the capacities that the client's workloads require. While these units aren't as flexible as GPUs, they provide far better cost performance than a GPU on properly configured workloads. This helps AI hyperscalers maximize their computing potential at lower cost, which is particularly appealing as funds become harder to come by.

Broadcom has several big-name clients, including Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Meta Platforms, Anthropic, and OpenAI. While all of its clients are ramping up their AI infrastructure spending, none have had a more successful product than Alphabet. Alphabet and Broadcom collaborated to design the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). This unit has been around for a while, and has gone through several generations. Google Cloud clients can rent access to TPUs on that computing platform. But TPUs are so impressive that Alphabet has begun to expand beyond leasing their compute power in its data centers, and is now starting to sell them directly to external customers like Meta as well.

title: Should You Buy Qualcomm Stock For Its Cash?
detail:
Should You Buy Qualcomm Stock For Its Cash?
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Over the last twelve months, Qualcomm (QCOM) generated free cash flow equal to 5.5% of its market value. That outpaces the 4.4% yield for the median S&P 500 company. A yield above the median can mean a business that is either on sale or expected to shrink. Qualcomm's revenue fell in each of its last two quarters. So is that cash the sign of a business on sale, or of one that is shrinking?

What A Qualcomm Share Gives You

Free cash flow represents the money Qualcomm retains from operations after covering plants and equipment. Every share provides a claim on that cash. Just like a share of the profits, that claim holds up whether the company distributes the cash or holds it. Any cash Qualcomm keeps remains the property of its shareholders.

Share prices generally rise to reflect the cash investors can see. They climb even faster when that cash pool is growing. For Qualcomm, the trajectory of its cash matters just as much as the total amount.

When Qualcomm is a large share of what you own, your plan leans on one company's cash flow. See how to protect a concentrated position.

How Qualcomm Earns From Chips And What It Owes

Qualcomm licenses its patents and sells chips for phones, cars and other devices. In fiscal 2025, the chip business brought in $38.4 billion of the company's $44.3 billion in revenue.

The company spends little to maintain these operations. Capital spending consumed just 16% of its cash from operations over the last twelve months. The $10.4 billion left over equalled 23.6% of revenue. While Qualcomm has kept its free cash flow above zero in every twelve-month period since mid-2023, the total has shrunk for two consecutive years. It hit $12.6 billion in the twelve months to June 2024, fell to $11.6 billion a year later and dropped to $10.4 billion in the twelve months to June 2026.

At the end of June 2026, Qualcomm owed $15.3 billion against $8.3 billion in cash and short-term investments. That gap equals 3.7% of its market value. Over the last twelve months, operating profit was 14.9 times interest costs.

Why Investors Doubt Qualcomm's Phone Chip Business

Qualcomm's revenue has started to fall, which may help explain why its yield sits above the median.
After dropping 3.5% in fiscal Q2, revenue fell another 4.0% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026. The operating margin also narrowed, slipping to 23.3% over the last twelve months from 28.2% a year earlier.

On the July 29, 2026 call, management said its phone chip sales reflected the effect of industry-wide memory prices on the smartphone market. Because of those prices and other input costs, chip gross margins will fall slightly below their usual range, management said. Qualcomm also said its share of the next iPhone launch would be materially lower than its earlier estimate of 20%. Moving forward, management forecast that revenue from Apple products would start stepping down faster in fiscal Q4 2026.

title: How much AMD stock does CEO Lisa Su actually own?
detail:
How much AMD stock does CEO Lisa Su actually own?
Dominic Diongson, Jeremy Salvucci
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 6:12 PM CDT 3 min read
AMD
Trade AMD on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Lisa Su joined Advanced Micro Devices in 2012, and two years later she was appointed CEO. She helped turn the financially struggling fabless chipmaker around by focusing on artificial intelligence and data centers. Toward the later part of 2026, AMD's market capitalization was nearing $1 trillion

Along the way, she was awarded large amounts of stock. Between her growing stake in the company (and its growing stock price), Su joined the ranks of tech CEO billionaires in 2024.

Here's how many AMD shares Su owns, and how she accumulated her holdings.

How much of AMD does Lisa Su own? 

Lisa Su owned 3.6 million shares, directly and indirectly via trusts, according to a September 2026 SEC filing. That equates to a 0.2% stake in the company. Those shares were valued at over $2 billion, as of a mid-October 2026 share price of around $562.23. 

Is Lisa Su the largest individual shareholder of AMD?

Lisa Su holds a larger AMD stake than any of the company's other current executives. The company insider with the next-largest stake is the company's Chief Technology Officer, Mark D. Papermaster, who owned 1,674,673 shares (less than half as many as Su) as of an August 2026 SEC filing.

Lisa Su may also be the biggest individual shareholder of AMD, but it is hard to say for sure. There may be individual shareholders who own more than she does, but if so, their ownership is less than 5%, and as such, they aren't required by SEC rules to disclose that information publicly. 

AMD's largest institutional shareholders

Institutions own the vast majority of AMD's stock, amounting to almost 83% of the total 1.63 billion in outstanding shares, according to Nasdaq. The Vanguard Group owned about 9.7%, and BlackRock owned about 9.2%, based on institutional holding data compiled by Nasdaq.

How & when did Lisa Su accumulate her AMD stock?

Lisa Su joined AMD as a senior vice president in 2012, and she quickly rose through the ranks to become CEO in 2014. Along the way, she was granted stock awards and performance-based restricted stock units (PRSUs).

In 2013, when she completed her first year at AMD, she was awarded 446,399 shares, according to the company's 2013 proxy statement.

In 2012, Lisa Su was paid $575,000 as a senior vice president, but stock awards and a cash bonus pushed up her total compensation to $6 million. About half of that compensation was in stock awards and a third of the total in stock options. By 2013, she held more than 400,000 shares.

title: Prediction: $1,000 Invested in Taiwan Semi (TSMC) Today Will Be Worth This Much by 2030.
detail:
Prediction: $1,000 Invested in Taiwan Semi (TSMC) Today Will Be Worth This Much by 2030.
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 4:25 PM CDT 5 min read
TSM
NVDA
AVGO
AMD

Trading disclosure

Over the past four years, a $1,000 investment in TSMC (NYSE: TSM), the world's largest contract chipmaker, would have grown to about $4,540. That multibagger gain was primarily driven by the rapid growth of the cloud infrastructure and AI markets.

Could a fresh $1,000 investment in TSMC grow to more than $4,500 again by the end of the decade? Let's review its catalysts, challenges, and valuations to see if it's possible.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Understanding TSMC's core advantages

TSMC manufactures the world's smallest, densest, and most power-efficient chips for fabless chipmakers like Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), AMD, and Broadcom. To maintain its lead over other foundries, TSMC purchases more extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems -- which are required for optically etching tiny circuit patterns onto silicon wafers -- from ASML (NASDAQ: ASML) than any other foundry.

Once a fabless chipmaker is locked into TSMC's manufacturing services, the astronomical switching costs prevent it from moving to a competing foundry such as Samsung or Intel (NASDAQ: INTC). TSMC also offers a higher yield (the percentage of functional chips per wafer) than other foundries. So while TSMC's competitors might offer lower manufacturing costs per wafer, their lower yields and tighter production bottlenecks can easily offset those savings.

TSMC's scale enables it to push ASML's current-gen "low-NA" EUV systems to their theoretical limits (to 1.4nm) before it needs to buy ASML's pricier "high-NA" EUV systems to produce even smaller chips. By comparison, Intel is making the leap to high-NA much earlier than TSMC -- but that expansion will be costly because those systems cost about twice as much as low-NA systems. By waiting until the early 2030s to ramp up its purchases of high-NA EUV systems, TSMC can wait for the technology to mature and become cheaper before making that leap.

In the third quarter of 2026, TSMC generated 68% of its revenue from the high-performance computing (HPC) market -- which includes Nvidia's data center GPUs and Broadcom's custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) for hyperscalers.

That segment's revenue surged 22% sequentially in the third quarter, accelerating from 20% sequential growth in the first and second quarters. That acceleration should continue as long as more companies upgrade their cloud and AI data centers. It also generated a third of its revenue from its smallest 3nm chips -- which include Nvidia's Vera Rubin (Vera CPU and Rubin GPU) chips and the base die of the latest high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips.

Taiwan Semiconductor slipped just 2%, outperforming the iShares Semiconductor ETF's 3% broader chip sector decline.

A Delaware jury verdict is adding to the pressure on Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) as a broad selloff in chip stocks extends its run. Arm stock is down 5% during afternoon trading, landing at $232.22. Similarly, shares of Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) are down 5% to $534.29, a move in line with Arm stock.

gorodenkoff / Getty Images

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) shares are down 2% to $412.45, a softer slide than Arm stock. Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) is the other party to the case and holds a chip architecture license from Arm. TSM's Snapdragon processors power a wide range of devices, and Qualcomm also runs a patent licensing business of its own.

Semiconductor names as a group are lower, as well. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is down 3%, a smaller drop than Arm stock or AMD shares. Large-cap tech is softer too, with the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) down 2%.

Delaware Jury Sides With Qualcomm on Key Claims

A federal jury in Delaware found on Tuesday that Arm breached its chip architecture license agreement with Qualcomm. Jurors also found that Arm interfered with Qualcomm's relationship with a customer and violated California's unfair competition law. Arm did prevail on a separate technology licensing claim, giving the company one win in an otherwise negative outcome.

(Updates with market moves at the end of the day, and other changes, if any.)

The Nasdaq Composite plunged Friday, halting its four-week rally, amid a technology sell-off on Wall Street.

The index declined 2.1% to 26,140.03. The S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,659.44, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.3% to 52,002.41.

Among sectors, tech led the laggards, while energy paced the gainers.

This week, the Nasdaq tumbled 4.5%, ending its four-week winning streak. That weekly performance marked the worst since June.

The S&P 500 ended the week down 1.9% and the Dow gained 0.7%.

Alphabet (GOOGL), Salesforce (CRM), Cisco Systems (CSCO), Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN), and Nvidia (NVDA) were the biggest decliners on the Dow.

Micron Technology (MU), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Sandisk (SNDK) also fell.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite hit fresh closing highs Oct. 6, but the rally had been powered by only a few tech giants, suggesting underlying weakness on Wall Street.

Many analysts fear a potential stock market correction as the majority of S&P 500 stocks have been hovering well below all-time highs.

Treasury yields were mixed. The two-year rate fell 3.2 basis points at 4.72%, while the 10-year rate was unchanged at 5.09%.

US industrial production grew more than expected in September as manufacturing output rebounded despite weakness in the auto component, Federal Reserve data showed.

Brent crude jumped 3.4% to $109.53 a barrel in Friday late-afternoon trade, while West Texas Intermediate was 3.8% higher at $101.64. Both benchmarks were up for the week, with Brent on track for its fourth consecutive weekly increase.

Saudi Arabia intercepted multiple missiles and drones on Friday, including a missile heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, CNBC reported, citing a military spokesperson.

US lawmakers introduced a bill Friday to block President Donald Trump's deal to allow export of hundreds of millions of barrels of Russian diesel, Bloomberg News reported.

Spot gold fell 0.1% to $4,166.56 per troy ounce, while silver remained steady at $57.14 per ounce.
